llm_reasoning.anomaly_A_headline: 346 employees (8.6%) show high skills yet are associated with failed projects — a critical inconsistency.
llm_reasoning.anomaly_B_headline: 949 employees with below-average skills achieved project success, reinforcing that teamwork, context and luck play significant roles.
reasons_for_anomaly_A: Lower engagement despite high skills — disengaged employees underperform in execution.
More conflict cases — team friction may derail otherwise skilled employees.
Higher overtime — burnout risk may reduce effective contribution despite high skill.
Poorer work-life balance — organizational stress dampens skilled output.
Lower training efficiency — skills exist but are not being applied effectively.
Project complexity mismatch — highly skilled employees placed on overly complex projects without adequate support.
Leadership or team dynamics issues — individual skill does not guarantee team-level project success.
Skills may be domain-specific and not aligned to the project type assigned.
External/organizational factors (deadlines, resources) — not captured by skill ratings alone.
llm_reasoning.key_insight: Skill ratings are necessary but not sufficient for project success. Engagement, work conditions, team dynamics and project-role alignment are critical mediating factors.
llm_reasoning.business_implication: Organizations should not rely solely on skill assessments for project staffing. Engagement, WLB, role-project alignment and team composition must be evaluated together.
llm_reasoning.project_complexity_note: Project complexity is mixed in failure cases (Simple ~39%, Complex ~31.5%), suggesting failure is not purely due to complexity but also organizational and execution factors — even simple projects fail when engagement and alignment are poor.
